rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Four families carry the syllabus: Brassicaceae — cruciform petals, tetradynamous stamens (2+4), replum-bearing siliqua (mustard, cabbage); Fabaceae — zygomorphic papilionaceous flowers, diadelphous stamens (9+1), marginal placentation, legume and Rhizobium nodules (pea, gram, lentil); Solanaceae — five epipetalous stamens, persistent calyx, oblique bicarpellary ovary, berries and capsules (tomato, potato, chili);…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Brassicaceae has a cruciform corolla and tetradynamous stamens, four long and two short, and a siliqua. Fabaceae has a papilionaceous flower, diadelphous stamens in a 9+1 bundle, a legume, and Rhizobium nodules.
Solanaceae has five stamens joined to the petals and a berry or a capsule, as in tomato and Datura. Liliaceae is the monocot of the four: six tepals, six stamens, and a superior ovary, as in onion.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Tepals vs petals:** tepals = undifferentiated sepals+petals (Liliaceae, monocots); petals are distinct from sepals in the dicot families.  ·  **Epipetalous vs epiphyllous:** stamens attached to the corolla (Solanaceae) vs attached to tepals (Liliaceae).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Match the organism to the character.  ·  A product does not move an organism into another kingdom.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Brassica campestris*** — mustard; Nepal's cooking-oil crop.  ·  ***Pisum sativum*** — pea; Mendel's experimental plant (link to genetics).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Short answer (2m):** What is a floral formula? **Answer.** A **symbolic shorthand** that summarises a flower in one line: bracteation, symmetry (⊕ actinomorphic / % zygomorphic), sex (⚥ bisexual), then the numbers, fusion and arrangement of **K** calyx, **C** corolla, **A** androecium, **G** gynoecium — brackets for fusion, underline…  ·  **Long answer (5m):** Describe Solanaceae with floral formula, diagram and economic importance. **Answer.** **Habit and leaf:** mostly herbs and shrubs; alternate, exstipulate, usually simple leaves. **Inflorescence:** **cymose** (axis ends in a flower, later flowers from lateral branches).…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The formula as fingerprint:** each family's floral formula encodes its diagnosis — read symmetry, merosity, fusion and carpel number and the family follows.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Brassicaceae: cruciform 4 petals, tetradynamous 6 stamens, replum + siliqua, parietal placentation — mustard, cabbage, radish.  ·  Fabaceae: papilionaceous zygomorphic flower, 10 diadelphous stamens, marginal placentation, legume, Rhizobium nodules — pea, gram, lentil, soybean.  ·  Solanaceae: 5 epipetalous stamens, persistent calyx, cymose inflorescence, oblique septum, axile placentation, berry/capsule — tomato, potato, chili, tobacco.  ·  Liliaceae: trimerous, 6 tepals, 6 epiphyllous stamens, tricarpellary axile, capsule, underground bulbs/rhizomes — onion, garlic, aloe, colchicum.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Mendel chose Pisum (Fabaceae) partly for its clearly distinguishable traits — a family character that shaped genetics.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: ***Solanum tuberosum*** — potato; underground stem tuber (morphology link).  ·  ***Allium cepa*** — onion; bulb; classic cytology material (root tips).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Diadelphous vs tetradynamous:** diadelphous = stamens fused into two bundles (9+1, Fabaceae); tetradynamous = six stamens in two lengths (2+4, Brassicaceae).  ·  **Siliqua vs legume:** siliqua = two-valved fruit with a false septum (replum) between parietal placentas (Brassicaceae); legume = one carpel dehiscing along both sutures (Fabaceae).  ·  Practise writing each formula with correct symbols — formulas carry dedicated marks in family questions.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: "A family is a hypothesis of common ancestry expressed in a floral formula."  ·  Why do legume fields need less nitrogen fertiliser? **Answer.** Because legumes **make their own nitrogen**. Nodules on their roots house ***Rhizobium*** bacteria, which possess **nitrogenase** — the only enzyme that converts atmospheric N₂ into ammonia the plant can use.…  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.
